paragraphs.text: This cake was made from leaf grown in Yiwu, in Yunnan.

The leaf was made into [ripe pu’er](shou:definition). After sun drying it was wetted and heaped in a [warm pile](shou:wet-piling), turned as the heat built over a month or two, then dried and pressed into a cake. Yunnan’s state factories brought that method into production in 1973. A ripe cake like this one is ready to drink now, without the years of keeping that raw pu’er usually asks for.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it, so the leaves stay whole. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water and forgives a heavy hand. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml, one quick rinse, then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
